# Task description

> In this task, we are going to use various **supervised learning methods** to try to predict the antibody response to influenza vaccination using early gene expression measurements.

> To save us some time, I have preprocessed the data for you. The data is an extract of open-access data from the Human Immune Project Consortium, with [detail of the study found here](https://immunespace.org/query/study/SDY1119#study-citations). The relevant information for this exercise is as follows :
>
> - Antibodies were measured at days 0 and 28
> - Gene expression of around 10,000 genes was measured at days 0 and 7

> Flu is an interesting virus in this context, since it is a common disease, and many people may have already been infected with a given flu strain prior to vaccination. There is evidence in the literature that prior infection can modify the response to vaccination. Therefore, to take into account baseline (day 0) information, I have transformed both the response and the predictors into (log2) fold-change values. That is, the *ratio* between the post-vaccination and pre-vaccination measurements.

> Our task will be to see if the day 7 fold-change of expression in some genes is predictive of the day 28 fold-change in antibody levels. That is, we seek to find an early gene expression signature which informs us of the later antibody response.

# Setup

## 0a) Set up your project

### Why do we need a project?

> When you analyse data in R, you need to tell R *where* files are. For example, you might load data into your environment by defining a path `"C:/Users/me/Documents/data/file.xlsx"`. However, this is problematic, since it is specific to your own computer setup. The code will then break as soon as you move the files, share them with a colleague, or re-run the analysis on a different machine.

> To avoid this, we will introduce some basic organisational skills for an R project. Firstly, we will contain the work in a single **R project folder** (the root), and refer to every file *relative to that folder*. This makes specifying paths for loading data and saving outputs more robust.

> Using a project folder also helps to organise files in a clean way.
>
> - **raw data** : the original data files, which you should never modify;
> - **analysis** : the code (such as this `.Rmd` file) that reads the raw data and produces results;
> - **output** : everything the code creates (figures, tables, processed data), which should be able to be perfectly regenerated by re-running the code.

### Create the project folder

> If you already created a project for a previous practical, you can reuse it : open it and go to "Add the files" below. Otherwise :

> 1. In RStudio, click `File > New Project... > New Directory > New Project`.
> 2. Give the project a name, for example `omics_practicals`, and choose where to save it on your computer. Click `Create Project`.
> 3. RStudio restarts inside your new project. You can check this in the top-right corner of RStudio, which now shows the project name, and in the `Files` pane, which shows a single file called e.g. `omics_practicals.Rproj`.

> Next, create three sub-folders inside the project. In the `Files` pane of RStudio, click `New Folder` and create `data-raw`, `analysis`, and `output`. Alternatively, run the following code once in the R console.

```{r, eval = F}
dir.create("data-raw")
dir.create("analysis")
dir.create("output")
```

> Your project should now look like this:

```
omics_practicals/
├── omics_practicals.Rproj    <- marks the "root" of the project
├── data-raw/                 <- the raw data files
├── analysis/                 <- the practicals (.Rmd files)
└── output/                   <- figures and results that you save
```

### Add the files

> 1. Copy the data file I sent you, `SDY1119_day7_GE_foldChange.RData`, into the `data-raw` folder.
> 2. Copy this practical (the `.Rmd` file) into the `analysis` folder.
> 3. In the `Files` pane of RStudio, open the `analysis` folder and click on the `.Rmd` file to open it.

> **Important:** always start your work by opening the project (double-click the `.Rproj` file, or use `File > Open Project`), and open the `.Rmd` file from *within* RStudio's `Files` pane. If you open the `.Rmd` file directly from your Downloads folder, it will not be part of the project and the paths below will not work.

### How do we refer to files?

> By default, R Markdown runs code from the folder where the `.Rmd` file is saved (here, `analysis/`), which would make paths confusing. Instead, we will use the `here` package. The function `here()` always returns the path to the root of your project (the folder containing the `.Rproj` file), wherever the code is run from. We then build paths from this root. For example, `here("data-raw", "my_file.RData")` points to `my_file.RData` inside the `data-raw` folder, and `here("output", "my_plot.pdf")` points to a file in the `output` folder. The same code works on any computer and operating system, and you never have to type a full path.

# 1) Ridge regression

## 1a) Nested cross-validation

> We are going to start by performing ridge regression in a (nested) cross-validation setup.

> The goal is to evaluate a given predictive model's performance on unseen data. The simplest approach to achieve this is a test-train split. Here, observations are randomly assigned to either the training set or the testing set. A model is trained on the training set, and used to predict on the unseen testing set. The predictions can then be compared to their true values to obtain an unbiased estimate of the model's performance. However, this approach uses data inefficiently and depends on the random splitting of the data.

> K-fold cross-validation is a better alternative to this approach. Here, we first split the data into K distinct *folds* (partitions of the data). Cross-validation is a loop, where in each stage, a different fold is chosen to act as the testing set. Therefore, K-fold cross-validation results in a series of K models and sets of predictions which can be used to evaluate the performance.

> Some models have *hyperparameters* to specify, which are parameters which control certain aspects of the learning process. Ridge regression and other penalised approaches use a hyperparameter which controls the strength of the penalisation term. Since we are unlikely to have much reason to prefer any particular values of these hyperparameters, we may prefer to let the data decide for us which are the *best* values. We can also do this with cross-validation.

> Typically, we do something called *nested cross-validation* in order to first build a model with optimal hyperparameters, and then use that model to predict on unseen data. A nested cross-validation has two loops. The first, called the *outer loop*, separates the training data from the testing data. The second, called the *inner loop*, uses cross-validation on the training data only to select the best values of the model hyperparameters, which are those that optimise a particular metric on the unseen inner loop testing data.

> Take the metric to optimise to be the root-mean-squared-error. That is,

$$
\text{RMSE} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2}
$$

> This can be computed with the following helper function, which takes a vector of observed values, and a vector of predicted values, and computes the RMSE.

```{r}
rmse <- function(obs, pred) {
  sqrt(mean((obs - pred) ^ 2, na.rm = TRUE))
}
```

> Data scaling is an important step in penalised regression. We should always scale the training and testing data *separately* to avoid "data leakage" : the testing data must not influence anything done to the training data. We scale each gene in the training data to have mean 0 and standard deviation 1, by subtracting its mean and dividing by its standard deviation. We then put the testing data on the same scale, by using the training means and standard deviations. The following helper function does this.

```{r}
scale_with_train <- function(X_train, X_test) {
  # Mean and standard deviation of each gene, in the training data only
  col_means <- colMeans(X_train)
  col_sds <- apply(X_train, 2, sd)

  # In case any gene is constant, set the standard deviation to 1 to avoid dividing by 0
  col_sds[col_sds == 0 | is.na(col_sds)] <- 1

  list(
    train = scale(X_train, center = col_means, scale = col_sds),
    test = scale(X_test, center = col_means, scale = col_sds)
  )
}
```

> The following function manually codes a nested cross-validation with a regularised regression model (ridge, lasso or elastic net) from the `glmnet` package. Read through the code and make sure you understand the underlying process - you will be reusing this function for the first part of the exercise.

```{r}
# Nested cross-validation of a glmnet model.
# X_mat : numeric matrix of predictors (rows are samples, columns are genes)
# y_vec : numeric vector of the response
# alpha : 0 for ridge regression, 1 for lasso regression
# lambda_grid : values of the hyperparameter lambda to choose from in the inner loop
# n_outer, n_inner : number of folds in the outer and inner loops
nested_cv_glmnet <- function(X_mat, y_vec, alpha, lambda_grid,
                             n_outer = 10, n_inner = 5, seed = 123) {
  set.seed(seed)
  n <- nrow(X_mat)

  # Create the outer-layer folds using the createFolds() function
  folds_outer <- createFolds(y_vec, k = n_outer, list = TRUE, returnTrain = FALSE)

  # Storage for the results of each fold, and for the prediction of each observation
  outer_results <- vector("list", n_outer)
  names(outer_results) <- paste0("fold", seq_len(n_outer))
  y_pred_all <- rep(NA_real_, n)

  # ---- Outer loop ----
  for (i in seq_len(n_outer)) {

    # The testing set is fold i, and the training set is all the other observations
    test_idx <- folds_outer[[i]]
    train_idx <- setdiff(seq_len(n), test_idx)

    X_train_outer <- X_mat[train_idx, ]
    y_train_outer <- y_vec[train_idx]
    X_test_outer <- X_mat[test_idx, ]
    y_test_outer <- y_vec[test_idx]

    # ---- Inner loop : choose the best lambda using the training data only ----

    # Create the inner folds : randomly permute the training row numbers, then cut them
    perm_inner <- sample(length(train_idx))
    folds_inner <- split(perm_inner,
                         cut(seq_along(perm_inner), breaks = n_inner, labels = FALSE))

    # Matrix of the RMSE of each inner fold (rows) for each value of lambda (columns)
    inner_rmse_mat <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = n_inner, ncol = length(lambda_grid))

    for (j in seq_len(n_inner)) {

      # The inner testing set is inner fold j. Careful : the indices in folds_inner are
      # relative to the training data, so we convert them to indices of the full data
      test_idx_in_train <- folds_inner[[j]]
      train_idx_in_train <- setdiff(seq_along(train_idx), test_idx_in_train)
      test_idx_full <- train_idx[test_idx_in_train]
      train_idx_full <- train_idx[train_idx_in_train]

      # Scale the inner training and testing data
      scaled_inner <- scale_with_train(X_mat[train_idx_full, ], X_mat[test_idx_full, ])

      # Fit the models with glmnet(), one for each value of lambda in lambda_grid
      fit_inner <- glmnet(
        x = scaled_inner$train,
        y = y_vec[train_idx_full],
        alpha = alpha,
        lambda = lambda_grid,
        standardize = TRUE,
        intercept = TRUE
      )

      # Predict on the inner testing set (one column of predictions per value of lambda),
      # and compute the RMSE of each
      preds_inner <- predict(fit_inner, newx = scaled_inner$test, s = lambda_grid)
      inner_rmse_mat[j, ] <- apply(preds_inner, 2, function(pred) rmse(y_vec[test_idx_full], pred))
    }

    # The best lambda minimises the mean RMSE across the inner folds
    mean_rmse_per_lambda <- colMeans(inner_rmse_mat, na.rm = TRUE)
    best_lambda <- lambda_grid[which.min(mean_rmse_per_lambda)]

    # ---- Fit the final model on the outer training data, using the best lambda ----
    scaled_outer <- scale_with_train(X_train_outer, X_test_outer)

    fit_outer <- glmnet(
      x = scaled_outer$train,
      y = y_train_outer,
      alpha = alpha,
      lambda = best_lambda,
      standardize = TRUE,
      intercept = TRUE
    )

    # Predict on the outer testing set, and store the predictions at the original positions
    preds_outer <- predict(fit_outer, newx = scaled_outer$test, s = best_lambda) %>%
      as.numeric()
    y_pred_all[test_idx] <- preds_outer

    test_rmse <- rmse(y_test_outer, preds_outer)

    outer_results[[i]] <- list(
      fold = i,
      test_idx = test_idx,
      best_lambda = best_lambda,
      mean_rmse_per_lambda = mean_rmse_per_lambda,
      test_rmse = test_rmse
    )

    # Print a message to keep us updated on the progress
    message(sprintf("Finished outer fold %d : selected lambda = %g, test RMSE = %0.4f",
                    i, best_lambda, test_rmse))
  }

  list(
    cv_results = data.frame(response = y_vec, predicted = y_pred_all),
    outer_results = outer_results
  )
}
```

> Let's use this function to perform ridge regression (`alpha = 0`) on all the genes. We choose the value of lambda from the following grid. The function returns a list. Its element `cv_results` is a data frame containing the true response of each participant, and the value predicted when this participant was in the outer testing set (that is, a prediction on unseen data).

```{r}
lambda_grid <- c(0.001, 0.005, 0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100)

ridge_all <- nested_cv_glmnet(
  X_mat = as.matrix(expression_all),
  y_vec = y_vec,
  alpha = 0,
  lambda_grid = lambda_grid
)

head(ridge_all$cv_results)
```

## 1b) Model evaluation

> Compute two metrics to evaluate the performance of your predictive models on the unseen data: the standardised root-mean-squared-error and the R2 statistic. We will need these metrics for all the models in this practical, so write a function `evaluate_predictions()` which takes the data frame of true and predicted values (`cv_results`) and returns the two metrics.

> The standardised RMSE is the RMSE of your predictions compared to the true values, divided by the standard deviation of the true values. The lower this value is, the better. If the sRMSE = 1, your predictions are as good on average as a model which simply predicts the response as the training sample mean (i.e. who does not use any of the predictor information). Anything less than 1 indicates a model which predicts better than this naïve model. The formula for the standardised RMSE is :

$$
\text{sRMSE} = \frac{\sqrt{\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2}}{sd(y)}
$$

> The R2 statistic is the squared Pearson correlation between the response and predicted values. The higher this is, the better. It can be interpreted as "the proportion of variability in the true response which is explained by the predictions". The formula is the following :

$$
R^{2} = cor_{\text{pearson}}(y, \hat{y})^{2}
$$

> Apply your function to the predictions of the ridge regression. In terms of these metrics, are you happy with the quality of these predictions?

<!-- solution:code -->
```{r}
evaluate_predictions <- function(cv_results) {
  # Standardised RMSE : the RMSE divided by the standard deviation of the response
  std_rmse <- rmse(cv_results$response, cv_results$predicted) / sd(cv_results$response)

  # R2 : the squared Pearson correlation between the response and the predictions
  r2 <- cor(cv_results$response, cv_results$predicted, method = "pearson") ^ 2

  data.frame(std_rmse = std_rmse, r2 = r2)
}

metrics_ridge_all <- evaluate_predictions(ridge_all$cv_results)
metrics_ridge_all
```
<!-- /solution -->

<!-- solution:text -->
> **Answer:** *[To write : are the standardised RMSE and R2 of the ridge regression satisfactory?]*
<!-- /solution -->

## 1c) Plot the results

> Now, using the `ggplot2` package, plot your predicted values against the true response values. Ensure that the x and y axes have the same limits and scale. Plot the "identity line" through the diagonal of the plot. This line shows where perfect predictions lie (i.e. predicted value = true value). As a bonus, annotate the plot with the metrics. Again, write this as a function `plot_predictions()`, which takes the data frame `cv_results`, the metrics, and a title, and returns the plot. Use it to plot the ridge regression predictions, and save the figure as a PDF in your `output` folder.

<!-- solution:code -->
```{r}
plot_predictions <- function(cv_results, metrics, title) {
  # Same limits for both axes : the range of the response and the predictions, with some padding
  results_range <- range(c(cv_results$response, cv_results$predicted))
  padding <- diff(results_range) * 0.02
  lims <- c(results_range[1] - padding, results_range[2] + padding)

  # Annotation with the metrics, in the top right corner
  label_txt <- sprintf("Std RMSE = %.3f\nR² = %.3f", metrics$std_rmse, metrics$r2)

  ggplot(cv_results, aes(x = response, y = predicted)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.7, size = 2) +
    geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "red", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) +
    coord_equal(xlim = lims, ylim = lims) +
    annotate("text", x = lims[2], y = lims[2], label = label_txt,
             hjust = 1, vjust = 1, size = 5) +
    labs(title = title, x = "True (observed)", y = "Predicted") +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold"))
}

plot_ridge_all <- plot_predictions(ridge_all$cv_results, metrics_ridge_all,
                                   "True vs predicted values (ridge regression, all genes)")

ggsave(here("output", "predictions_ridge_all.pdf"), plot_ridge_all, width = 8, height = 8)

plot_ridge_all
```
<!-- /solution -->

## 1d) Variable filtration

> Ridge regression can handle multicollinearity, but suffers in the (very) high-dimensional setting. This is because the penalisation term in ridge regression is incapable of reducing the variable coefficients to 0, and thus, every input variable contributes to the final model. Therefore, ridge regression tends to accumulate noise in very high-dimensional settings.

> A simple way to reduce the dimension of the data prior to predictive modelling could be to apply some kind of variable filter. For example, we could make a hypothesis that the most variable genes are likely to be the genes which contribute the most in terms of predictive information.

> Write a function `mostvariable_predictors()` which takes the data frame of gene expression and a proportion, and returns the names of the genes which are in the top proportion of predictors by variance.

<!-- solution:code -->
```{r}
mostvariable_predictors <- function(expression, proportion) {
  # Variance of each gene
  gene_vars <- colVars(as.matrix(expression))
  names(gene_vars) <- colnames(expression)

  # Names of the genes with the highest variances
  n_keep <- floor(proportion * length(gene_vars))
  names(sort(gene_vars, decreasing = TRUE))[seq_len(n_keep)]
}
```
<!-- /solution -->

> Make a new data frame of predictors by selecting only the top 10% of most variable genes. Now, run the nested cross-validation again using the filtered predictors. Evaluate the predictions and plot them (using your functions from 1b and 1c, and saving the figure). How do your results change?

<!-- solution:code -->
```{r}
# The names of the top 10% of genes by variance, and the filtered predictors
genes_filtered <- mostvariable_predictors(expression_all, 0.1)
expression_filtered <- expression_all[, genes_filtered]

ridge_filtered <- nested_cv_glmnet(
  X_mat = as.matrix(expression_filtered),
  y_vec = y_vec,
  alpha = 0,
  lambda_grid = lambda_grid
)

metrics_ridge_filtered <- evaluate_predictions(ridge_filtered$cv_results)
metrics_ridge_filtered

plot_ridge_filtered <- plot_predictions(ridge_filtered$cv_results, metrics_ridge_filtered,
                                        "True vs predicted values (ridge regression, filtered genes)")

ggsave(here("output", "predictions_ridge_filtered.pdf"), plot_ridge_filtered, width = 8, height = 8)

plot_ridge_filtered
```
<!-- /solution -->

<!-- solution:text -->
> **Answer:** *[To write : how do the results change when only the 10% most variable genes are used?]*
<!-- /solution -->

Evaluate and plot the predictions, and save the figure. How does this compare to ridge?

# 3) The `caret` package

## 3a) Using `caret` to automate hyperparameter tuning

> In the previous exercises, we hard-coded nested cross-validation to explicitly see how CV can be used both to tune model hyperparameters and to make unbiased predictions on unseen data. Since ridge and lasso regression are both implemented in the same package, it was easy to reuse the code to run a different type of regression. In addition, we only had one hyperparameter to tune, lambda, which rendered the inner cross-validation loop relatively easy to hard-code.

> However, typically, different models are implemented in different packages in R, each with their own syntax. In addition, many models have 2 or more hyperparameters to tune, and it could get a bit messy to code the inner CV loop from scratch.

> Luckily, the `caret` package exists to automate hyperparameter tuning. Caret standardises syntax across packages to allow for many predictive models to be easily implemented. The other advantage is that it can make use of parallel processing so that we can speed up this process by using multiple cores at the same time.

> To train models and find the best hyperparameter(s), we use the `train()` function in `caret`. This function takes the following main arguments :
>
> - `x` : the matrix or data frame of predictors (columns) by samples (rows)
> - `y` : the vector of responses
> - `method` : the name of the regression method to be used. A full list of methods implemented in caret [can be found here](https://topepo.github.io/caret/available-models.html). For lasso regression, the method name is "glmnet".
> - `preProcess` : defines how the data should be pre-processed. Here, we will set this argument to `c("center", "scale")` to tell it to center and scale our data.
> - `tuneGrid` : a data frame where each column is a named hyperparameter from the method, and each row is a unique combination of these hyperparameters to be used to fit a model to the training data.
> - `trControl` : an object created using the `trainControl()` function which defines how the tuning process should be performed (e.g. in this practical, we have been using 5-fold cross-validation to tune our hyperparameters).
> - `metric` : the metric to be optimised when choosing the *best* model. We will stick to RMSE here.

> If we want caret to make use of parallel processing, we have to *register* the cores we are willing to commit beforehand using the `doParallel` package. The total number of cores on your system can be detected with the `detectCores()` function. In the following function, I am conservative, and register half of the available cores. Feel free to experiment and push this a bit closer to your maximum. We must not forget to stop the parallel computing backend at the end, or R could crash later on : the function does this for us.

> Read through the following function, which performs the same nested cross-validation as before using `caret`, and try to understand how caret is being used to implement the hyperparameter tuning. You will reuse it for the next models. Run the chunk to define the function.

```{r}
# Nested cross-validation of any model supported by caret.
# X_df : data frame of predictors (rows are samples, columns are genes)
# y_vec : numeric vector of the response
# method : name of the caret method (e.g. "glmnet", "pcr", "pls")
# tune_grid : data frame with a column per hyperparameter, and a row per combination to try
nested_cv_caret <- function(X_df, y_vec, method, tune_grid,
                            n_outer = 10, n_inner = 5,
                            n_cores = max(1, floor(detectCores() / 2)), seed = 123) {
  set.seed(seed)

  # Register the cores for parallel processing, and stop them when the function ends
  cl <- makeCluster(n_cores)
  registerDoParallel(cl)
  on.exit({
    stopCluster(cl)
    registerDoSEQ()
  })

  # Create the outer folds
  folds_outer <- createFolds(y_vec, k = n_outer, list = TRUE, returnTrain = FALSE)

  # Storage for the results of each fold, and for the prediction of each observation
  outer_results <- vector("list", n_outer)
  names(outer_results) <- paste0("fold", seq_len(n_outer))
  y_pred_all <- rep(NA_real_, length(y_vec))

  # Define how the tuning (the inner loop) should be done
  inner_ctrl <- trainControl(
    method = "cv",         # Cross-validation
    number = n_inner,      # Number of folds
    returnResamp = "none"  # Do not keep the metrics of each inner fold
  )

  # ---- Outer loop ----
  for (i in seq_len(n_outer)) {

    # The testing set is fold i, and the training set is all the other observations
    test_idx <- folds_outer[[i]]
    train_idx <- setdiff(seq_len(nrow(X_df)), test_idx)

    X_train <- X_df[train_idx, , drop = FALSE]
    y_train <- y_vec[train_idx]
    X_test <- X_df[test_idx, , drop = FALSE]
    y_test <- y_vec[test_idx]

    # caret::train() will :
    # - center and scale the data (preProcess),
    # - perform the inner CV to choose the best hyperparameters in tune_grid,
    # - return the model fitted on the whole training set using the best hyperparameters
    fit <- train(
      x = X_train,
      y = y_train,
      method = method,
      preProcess = c("center", "scale"),
      tuneGrid = tune_grid,
      trControl = inner_ctrl,
      metric = "RMSE"
    )

    # Predict on the outer testing set (caret applies the same pre-processing)
    preds <- predict(fit, newdata = X_test)
    y_pred_all[test_idx] <- preds

    test_rmse <- rmse(y_test, preds)

    outer_results[[i]] <- list(
      fold = i,
      test_idx = test_idx,
      best_tune = fit$bestTune,
      inner_results = fit$results,
      test_rmse = test_rmse
    )

    # Print a message to keep us updated on the progress
    best_tune_txt <- paste(names(fit$bestTune), unlist(fit$bestTune), sep = " = ", collapse = ", ")
    message(sprintf("Finished outer fold %d : selected %s, test RMSE = %0.4f",
                    i, best_tune_txt, test_rmse))
  }

  list(
    cv_results = data.frame(response = y_vec, predicted = y_pred_all),
    outer_results = outer_results
  )
}
```

> Here is how this function can be used to implement lasso regression on the full dataset. In `glmnet`, lasso regression corresponds to `alpha = 1`, which we must define in the tuning grid. Note : you do not need to run this code, as it could be quite long since the genes are not filtered beforehand.

```{r, eval = F}
lasso_all <- nested_cv_caret(
  X_df = expression_all,
  y_vec = y_vec,
  method = "glmnet",
  tune_grid = expand.grid(alpha = 1, lambda = lambda_grid)
)
```

# 5) Model interpretability

> In the previous exercises, we have focused on code implementation and on maximising the predictive accuracy of the models. However, an important part of predictive analysis is the interpretation of any *predictive signatures*. Different regression methods may have different natural ways to interpret the predictive importance of the input variables on the response. For example, in multiple linear regression, we can interpret the effect size estimates, confidence intervals, and p-values for a test of non-zero effect size. Random forest has a metric called variable importance, which tells us the loss in predictive accuracy when a given variable's values are randomly permuted.

## 5a) Interpretation of Lasso

> When using L1-regularised methods like lasso and elastic net, we may choose to interpret the predictors which have non-zero coefficients (i.e. the selected variables).

> Fit a tuned lasso regression model using `caret::train()` on the entire dataset (i.e. ignore cross-validation for now). The *final model* (i.e. which corresponds to the model with the hyperparameters which produce the lowest CV-RMSE) can be accessed from the `$finalModel` argument of the `train()` object, and the corresponding lambda value from the `$lambdaOpt` argument of the final model.

> Extract the coefficients of the model corresponding to this lambda using the `coef()` function on the final model with argument `s` equal to your best value of lambda. How many genes have non-zero coefficients? Can you think of a way to interpret these gene names to see if there are any particular biological processes which are over-represented?

<!-- solution:code -->
```{r}
# Fit and tune the lasso model on the whole dataset (alpha = 1), using 5-fold cross-validation
lasso_fit <- train(
  x = expression_all,
  y = y_vec,
  method = "glmnet",
  preProcess = c("center", "scale"),
  tuneGrid = expand.grid(alpha = 1, lambda = lambda_grid),
  trControl = trainControl(method = "cv", number = 5, returnResamp = "none"),
  metric = "RMSE"
)

# The final model, and its best lambda
lasso_final <- lasso_fit$finalModel
lasso_best_lambda <- lasso_final$lambdaOpt

# The coefficients at this lambda. The output of coef() is not particularly nice,
# so we convert it into a data frame
lasso_coef_mat <- as.matrix(coef(lasso_final, s = lasso_best_lambda))

lasso_coefs <- data.frame(
  name = rownames(lasso_coef_mat),
  coefficient = as.numeric(lasso_coef_mat[, 1])
)

# The genes with non-zero coefficients (excluding the intercept)
lasso_gene_signature <- lasso_coefs %>%
  filter(coefficient != 0, name != "(Intercept)") %>%
  pull(name)

message(length(lasso_gene_signature), " genes were selected.")

lasso_gene_signature

# To interpret these genes, we could paste their names, separated by commas, into software
# which finds the biological functions they represent (for example DAVID bioinformatics,
# or even generative AI tools can give a quick idea)
paste(lasso_gene_signature, collapse = ", ")
```
<!-- /solution -->

<!-- solution:text -->
> **Answer:** *[To write : the number of selected genes, and how to interpret them.]*
<!-- /solution -->

## 5b) Interpretation of sPLS

> Sparse partial least squares is an approach which uses L1 (lasso) regularisation on the weighting vectors in a partial least squares approach. That is, it finds sparse components which are maximally covarying with the response variable. We are going to implement this model using the `mixOmics` package. Unfortunately, this implementation is not available in `caret`, so we will have to use `mixOmics`'s internal functions to tune the model. The first hyperparameter to tune here is called `keepX`, which tells us how many variables to select for each component. This is roughly equivalent to tuning the strength of the penalty term, like we have done previously in this exercise. The second hyperparameter to choose is called `ncomp`, which tells us how many final components we should keep.

> Read the sPLS (regression) example on the [mixOmics site](https://mixomics.org/parameter-tuning/), and use the `mixOmics::tune.spls()` function on the entire dataset to determine the best values of `ncomp` and `keepX` (again, forget about the cross-validation framework for now). Save the plot of the tuning results.

> Note : there is a [known bug in the sPLS implementation in the regression setting](https://mixomics-users.discourse.group/t/error-in-check-entry-pls-x-y-ncomp-keepx-keepy-mode-mode-scale-scale-unmapped-y-contains-samples-with-no-associated-class-may-be-caused-by-nas-in-input-y-vector/1202/7), which may give you an error `Unmapped Y contains samples with no associated class`. This seems to be a problem when some values of the response are 0 : a workaround is to add a small value like 0.000001 to the response values, and the error should go away.

<!-- solution:code -->
```{r}
# The response as a matrix, with the workaround for the known bug
y_spls <- as.matrix(y_vec) + 0.000001

# Number of variables to keep that we want to try
keepX_grid <- c(1:10, seq(15, 50, 5))

spls_tuning <- mixOmics::tune.spls(
  X = expression_all,
  Y = y_spls,
  ncomp = 5,
  test.keepX = keepX_grid,
  scale = TRUE,
  validation = "Mfold",
  folds = 5,
  measure = "MSE",
  mode = "regression",
  nrepeat = 5
)

# Plot the tuning results, and save the plot as a PDF
plot(spls_tuning)

pdf(here("output", "spls_tuning.pdf"), width = 8, height = 6)
print(plot(spls_tuning))
invisible(dev.off())

# The best number of components, and the best number of variables to keep for each
spls_best_ncomp <- spls_tuning$choice.ncomp[[1]]
spls_best_keepX <- spls_tuning$choice.keepX[seq_len(spls_best_ncomp)]
```
<!-- /solution -->

> Now, with your best values of `ncomp` and `keepX`, fit a final model to the entire data. Extract the loading weights for the first latent variable and find the names of the genes with non-zero loading weights. How can we interpret these genes? [The following guide may help](https://mixomics.org/methods/spls/).

<!-- solution:code -->
```{r}
spls_final <- mixOmics::spls(expression_all, y_spls, keepX = spls_best_keepX, ncomp = spls_best_ncomp)

# The genes with non-zero loading weights on the first component
spls_gene_signature <- mixOmics::selectVar(spls_final, comp = 1)$X$name

paste(spls_gene_signature, collapse = ", ")

# Plot the loading weights of these genes, and save the plot as a PDF
mixOmics::plotLoadings(spls_final, method = "mean", contrib = "max")

pdf(here("output", "spls_loadings.pdf"), width = 8, height = 8)
mixOmics::plotLoadings(spls_final, method = "mean", contrib = "max")
invisible(dev.off())
```
<!-- /solution -->

<!-- solution:text -->
> **Answer:** *[To write : how to interpret the genes selected by sPLS.]*
<!-- /solution -->

## 5c) Stability Selection

> K-fold cross-validation complicates model interpretation, since, instead of having one model to interpret, we now have K models, each fit on different parts of the data, possibly using different hyperparameter values, and therefore using different selected variables.

> With L1-regularisation methods like lasso and elastic net, a solution is to interpret the *proportion of folds in which each variable is selected*. These approaches can broadly be called *stability selection* methods, as variables which are more frequently selected are more *stable* predictors.

> The goal of this final question is to implement elastic net regression in a cross-validation setup, and assess the stability of the variables selected. Modify the function `nested_cv_caret()` such that, during each outer fold, you store the names of the selected genes (i.e. those with non-zero coefficients). Run elastic net regression with it, as in 3b. Then, make a plot which shows the proportion of selection on one axis, and the gene names on the other axis (sorted from most frequently selected to least frequently selected). Save the plot.

> How could you derive a *stable* predictive gene signature from this plot?

<!-- solution:code -->
```{r}
# Same function as nested_cv_caret(), with the lines marked "NEW" added
nested_cv_caret_selection <- function(X_df, y_vec, method, tune_grid,
                                      n_outer = 10, n_inner = 5,
                                      n_cores = max(1, floor(detectCores() / 2)), seed = 123) {
  set.seed(seed)

  cl <- makeCluster(n_cores)
  registerDoParallel(cl)
  on.exit({
    stopCluster(cl)
    registerDoSEQ()
  })

  folds_outer <- createFolds(y_vec, k = n_outer, list = TRUE, returnTrain = FALSE)

  outer_results <- vector("list", n_outer)
  names(outer_results) <- paste0("fold", seq_len(n_outer))
  y_pred_all <- rep(NA_real_, length(y_vec))

  inner_ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = n_inner, returnResamp = "none")

  for (i in seq_len(n_outer)) {
    test_idx <- folds_outer[[i]]
    train_idx <- setdiff(seq_len(nrow(X_df)), test_idx)

    X_train <- X_df[train_idx, , drop = FALSE]
    y_train <- y_vec[train_idx]
    X_test <- X_df[test_idx, , drop = FALSE]
    y_test <- y_vec[test_idx]

    fit <- train(
      x = X_train,
      y = y_train,
      method = method,
      preProcess = c("center", "scale"),
      tuneGrid = tune_grid,
      trControl = inner_ctrl,
      metric = "RMSE"
    )

    # NEW : the genes with non-zero coefficients in the final model of this fold
    coef_mat <- as.matrix(coef(fit$finalModel, s = fit$bestTune$lambda))
    selected_genes <- setdiff(rownames(coef_mat)[coef_mat[, 1] != 0], "(Intercept)")

    preds <- predict(fit, newdata = X_test)
    y_pred_all[test_idx] <- preds

    test_rmse <- rmse(y_test, preds)

    outer_results[[i]] <- list(
      fold = i,
      test_idx = test_idx,
      best_tune = fit$bestTune,
      inner_results = fit$results,
      test_rmse = test_rmse,
      selected_genes = selected_genes   # NEW
    )

    message(sprintf("Finished outer fold %d : %d genes selected, test RMSE = %0.4f",
                    i, length(selected_genes), test_rmse))
  }

  list(
    cv_results = data.frame(response = y_vec, predicted = y_pred_all),
    outer_results = outer_results
  )
}

enet_selection <- nested_cv_caret_selection(
  X_df = expression_filtered,
  y_vec = y_vec,
  method = "glmnet",
  tune_grid = enet_grid
)

# The proportion of outer folds in which each gene was selected
n_outer <- length(enet_selection$outer_results)
selection_counts <- table(unlist(lapply(enet_selection$outer_results, `[[`, "selected_genes")))

selection_prop <- data.frame(
  gene = names(selection_counts),
  prop = as.numeric(selection_counts) / n_outer
) %>%
  arrange(desc(prop))

# Keep the genes selected in more than 50% of the folds
selection_prop_stable <- selection_prop %>%
  filter(prop > 0.5)

message(nrow(selection_prop_stable), " genes were selected in more than 50% of the folds.")

# Plot the selection proportions, from the most to the least frequently selected, and save it
selection_plot <- ggplot(selection_prop_stable, aes(x = reorder(gene, desc(prop)), y = prop)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "Gene",
       y = "Proportion of outer folds in which the gene is selected",
       title = "Selection frequency across the outer folds (> 50%)") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, vjust = 1, size = 8))

ggsave(here("output", "stability_selection.pdf"), selection_plot, width = 12, height = 6)

selection_plot
```
<!-- /solution -->

<!-- solution:text -->
> **Answer:** *[To write : how to derive a stable predictive gene signature from this plot.]*
<!-- /solution -->
